title: Interface Metaphor
body:
An **interface metaphor** borrows structure from something the user already understands. The
desktop metaphor is the largest example: files sit in folders on a desk, get dragged to a
wastebasket, and the whole arrangement lets somebody who has used an office understand a
computer.

The borrowed structure carries expectations, which is the benefit and the cost. A user who
knows folders expects that a file is in one place, that moving it out of a folder removes it
from there, and that the wastebasket holds things until it is emptied. Where the software
departs from the metaphor, the user is misled by exactly the thing meant to help them, which is
why a file appearing in two folders at once is confusing where a symbolic link is not.

```
metaphor that holds      folders, the wastebasket, the clipboard
metaphor that leaks      a "page" that never finishes loading
                         a "desktop" whose files are on somebody else's computer
```

A metaphor is a starting point, and it stops binding once the convention is learned. Once a
convention is learned it operates as a symbol in its own right, which is what happened to the
save icon in [[Skeuomorphism]], and at that point matching the physical original stops
mattering.
